summary: Sweden is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorization is not yet in operation), and everyone else applies for a €90 Schengen short-stay visa through the Swedish Migration Agency's consular network.

declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. tips.text: Bring a debit or credit card: the UK government's travel advice says many shops, cafes and restaurants in Sweden do not accept cash.

Under Sweden's Alcohol Act (2010:1622), retail sale of spirits, wine and strong beer is reserved for a state-owned company (Systembolaget), apart from the limited farm sales the Act allows, and alcohol may not be sold to anyone under 20.

Canada's travel advice says the right of public access (allemansrätten) lets you move and camp on public land, but not within 70 m of a dwelling or cultivated land, and that some areas, seasons and uses are restricted.

The UK government's travel advice says snow and ice cause road accidents daily in winter, and that all vehicles must have winter tyres from 1 December to 31 March and at any other time the police designate.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Sweden?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Around 60 nationalities — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — visit visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa applied for via the Swedish mission serving their place of residence.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Sweden?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Sweden and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Sweden Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11, and allows up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries. For visits of more than 90 days, the Swedish Migration Agency says you need a visitor's residence permit.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Sweden?
faq.answer: ETIAS for visa-exempt travelers is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Once mandatory, the €20 online authorization will be required before boarding.

faq.question: Can I pay with cash in Sweden?
faq.answer: Often not. The UK government's travel advice says many shops, cafes and restaurants do not accept cash, so make sure you have a debit or credit card with you, and Canada's travel advice says many shops and restaurants no longer accept cash.
